analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, estate, and gift taxes with a 20% flat tax and caps entitlement spending growth until 2002.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee: introduced in July 1995 by Senator Shelby with two Republican cosponsors, it got no markup, no vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would scrap the current income tax and replace it with a single flat rate — 20%, dropping to 17% — applied only to wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits, with a large standard deduction. All income from investments — interest, dividends, capital gains, rents — would go untaxed, and the estate and gift tax would be repealed entirely. It would also cap the growth of entitlement spending like Medicare, food stamps, and veterans' benefits at inflation plus population growth, with automatic across-the-board cuts if the cap was breached, and require a three-fifths vote of Congress to raise any tax rate or reduce the standard deduction.
analysis.who_benefits: The biggest winners would be households with large investment income, since only wages, pensions, and unemployment checks would be taxed while interest, dividends, and capital gains went untaxed, and the estate and gift tax repeal would benefit large inheritances. Employers with overfunded pension plans could reclaim excess assets, and retirement plans would no longer have to meet nondiscrimination rules protecting rank-and-file workers. Low-wage working families would also gain from the very large standard deductions — $21,400 for a married couple plus $5,000 per dependent — though they would lose the earned income tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners with investment income and large estates

how_it_helps.text: A family of four earning under roughly $63,000 would owe no income tax under the large standard deductions ($21,400 for joint filers plus $5,000 per dependent) [S3].
The tax code would be dramatically simpler: the alternative minimum tax, most tax credits, the estate and gift tax, and most of the rest of the individual income tax code would be repealed [S2] [S3].
Businesses would pay one flat rate on business income with no special deductions, replacing the corporate tax for corporations and pass-through businesses alike [S2] [S3].
The bill would require a balanced budget by fiscal year 2002, enforced by hard spending caps through 2002 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Low-income households would lose the earned income tax credit, repealed along with the rest of the tax credits, and low-income benefit programs (AFDC, food stamps, Medicaid, SSI) could be cut by up to 1% under automatic sequestration. Medicare payments could be cut by up to 4% under the spending caps. Middle-class families would lose the mortgage interest and charitable deductions, and homeowners and investors would face a new tax on the value of employer-provided health and fringe benefits. Rank-and-file workers would lose nondiscrimination and contribution limits that keep retirement plans from favoring executives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-income families, Medicare beneficiaries, and middle-class homeowners

drawbacks.text: All tax credits would be repealed, including the earned income tax credit, which is a wage subsidy for low-income working families; combined with benefit cuts of up to 1% for AFDC, food stamps, Medicaid, and SSI, the bill would hit poor households on both ends [S2] [S3].

Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation would be taxed, so income from wealth — capital gains, dividends, interest — would go untaxed while the estate and gift tax is repealed, concentrating the tax cut at the top [S2] [S3].

The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, coverage requirements, and contribution limits, and lets employers pull excess assets out of pension plans, removing protections that keep retirement plans from being designed around executives [S2] [S3].

Medicare payments could be automatically cut by up to 4% under the entitlement caps, and the spending caps would bite hardest when the economy slowed, forcing deeper cuts to benefits just when need was rising [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real and the large standard deductions would genuinely remove many low-wage families from the tax rolls. But the bill's largest benefits flow to households whose income comes from investments and to large estates, while the costs fall on low-income families (losing the earned income tax credit and facing benefit cuts), Medicare beneficiaries, and middle-class homeowners who lose the mortgage interest deduction. The three-fifths supermajority requirement for any tax change would also make it very hard for a future Congress to undo the distribution. On balance the design shifts the tax burden away from wealth and toward work and benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee in July 1995, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Shelby introduced the bill on July 19, 1995, with Senators Craig and Helms joining as cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee [S3] [S4] [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on the bill before the Congress ended in January 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing progressive tax code, the earned income tax credit, and the pension nondiscrimination rules all stayed in place, and Medicare and low-income benefit programs were spared the bill's automatic cuts. The people better off are the low-income and middle-income households who would have borne those costs; the households that would have gained from untaxed investment income and estate tax repeal are not better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Beneficiaries of the existing tax code and entitlement programs

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, the sole sponsor, and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

for.name: Sens. Larry Craig and Jesse Helms
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators joined [S3] [S4].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by Sen. Bob Packwood)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on July 19, 1995 and never scheduled a markup or reported it out; it sat until the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and the bill drew no Democratic support; it never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits would be taxed, leaving capital gains, dividends, and interest untaxed, and the estate and gift tax would be repealed — a large tax shift toward the wealthiest families, paid for partly by cutting low-income benefits and Medicare.

The bill repeals pension nondiscrimination and coverage rules and lets employers reclaim excess pension assets with only income tax owed, shifting retirement plans' protections away from rank-and-file workers.
Medicare payments could be automatically cut by up to 4% under the entitlement spending caps, reducing provider revenue at the same time beneficiaries face reduced access.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and state and local governments
industries.note: Employers that do not owe the business tax — charities, governments — would pay a new 20% tax on the value of noncash fringe benefits like health insurance they provide employees, raising the cost of hiring.
